opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic argument is pretty simple, and it's almost a selection argument. If you have a bunch of different actors (states, companies, eventually AI systems themselves), and some of them are willing to put everything into growth and power, and others are willing to spend some of their resources on things we'd call intrinsically valuable, like leisure, art, caring for people who aren't economically productive, then over long enough time scales the ones that maximise for growth tend to outcompete the others. It's not that anyone has to be evil. It's just that whatever spends less on "slack" grows faster, and eventually it's the thing that's left.

Historically, we've been somewhat protected from the worst of this, because humans were necessary. States needed citizens to fight wars and pay taxes, and companies needed workers and consumers. That gave ordinary people a kind of bargaining power, and a lot of what we think of as liberal values partly rode on top of that. Once AI can do essentially everything humans do, and do it better and cheaper, that implicit leverage goes away. The competitive pressure to just route around humans gets much stronger, and there's much less pushing back.

Now, the obvious response is: fine, so we coordinate. We build a world government or some sort of singleton that can say "no, we're not going to race to the bottom." I take that seriously, and I think it's maybe our best hope. But I'm pessimistic about it being the default for a few reasons. One, coordination itself is costly, and the coordinating entity also faces internal competition: factions, successors, pressure to stay strong relative to potential defectors. Two, even if you get a singleton, it has to stay aligned with human interests indefinitely, over a period where humans are contributing basically nothing, and it's not clear what keeps it honest. And three, there's always the outside view. Space is big, and if any part of civilisation decides not to hold back, that's the part that expands.

So when I say I think competition is likely to win at the highest level, I don't mean it's a law of physics. I mean that absent a really deliberate, robust, and frankly unprecedented effort to lock in some kind of cooperative structure that actually values humans for their own sake, the default trajectory is one where whatever is most fit for growth inherits the future. And there's no particular reason to expect that to be us, or to care much about us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses humans’ historical bargaining power and the difficulty of maintaining a singleton, but does not say that historical attempts to lock in values have always failed.

r002.rationale: It notes competition within a coordinating entity and from potential defectors, but does not claim that adding more levels of civilisational scaffolding also adds more levels of competition.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic picture I have is something like: even if we get alignment right in the narrow sense — the systems do what their operators want — we still haven't solved the problem of what happens when you have lots of operators, lots of systems, all under selection pressure. And I think the default outcome of that is that competition sets the terms, not any particular human's values.

The reason is pretty simple. If there's any variation in how much different actors are willing to sacrifice for efficiency, for growth, for influence, then the ones who sacrifice more tend to end up with more. That's true of companies, it's true of nations, it's historically been true of basically every scale of human organisation. And the thing that's kept it in check so far is that humans are the bottleneck. You need people to run the factories, to staff the army, to pay the taxes. So states and firms had to keep humans reasonably happy and healthy and educated, because that's where the productive capacity came from. That constraint gave us a lot of what we'd call good outcomes, kind of as a byproduct.

Once AI can do most of that work, that leverage goes away. The thing I keep coming back to is: what would a state or a company actually have to give up to keep looking after its people? And the answer is, more and more, "a competitive edge." And in a competitive environment, whoever is willing to give up less wins. So you'd expect a gradual drift — not necessarily anyone deciding to be evil, just everyone making locally reasonable decisions — where more and more of the resources and decision-making flow to whatever wins, and less and less to whatever we actually care about.

I should say I don't think this is inevitable. You can imagine coordination — a world government, or a small number of actors who can agree to carve out space for human flourishing and actually enforce it. But coordination at that scale is really hard and historically rare, and the competitive dynamic is the thing that happens if you don't do anything. That's why I think it's the default, and I think that's worth being pretty worried about even in the world where the technical alignment problem goes well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses historical competitive dynamics and human constraints, but it does not say that attempts to lock in values have always failed.

r002.rationale: It describes competition among many actors and systems, but does not claim that adding levels of civilisational scaffolding adds levels of competition.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic worry is that being able to coordinate doesn’t necessarily make coordination stable. You can imagine a civilisation where everyone agrees, “We have enough. Let’s stop expanding and spend our resources on having good lives.” But if some group instead uses those resources to grow, make copies of itself, and acquire more power, then over time it can become a larger fraction of that civilisation.

That doesn’t require everyone to be competitive. It only requires there to be some competitive actors, and for the others to be unable to constrain them. And the things that help you win that competition aren’t necessarily the things we care about. Producing happy lives might be a cost that a more competitive system dispenses with.

Now, that’s not an argument that cooperation is impossible. We do manage to suppress lots of destructive competition through institutions. But you need something that enforces the agreement, and that enforcement has to remain effective as the civilisation grows and changes. So my concern is that competition is the default pressure, whereas keeping it contained is an ongoing achievement. I’m not sure it has to win, but I don’t think we can assume that greater intelligence or greater abundance will make that pressure disappear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of keeping cooperation stable, but does not say that historical attempts to lock in values have always failed.

r002.rationale: It says competition can persist despite coordination and institutions, but does not propose that adding levels of civilisational scaffolding adds levels of competition.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure it will, but the basic argument is that cooperation has to be maintained, whereas competition can emerge whenever there are groups that can act independently. Even if almost everyone agrees to limit growth or leave some resources untouched, a group that doesn’t accept those limits can expand and eventually become much more powerful.

That doesn’t mean the competitors have to be especially aggressive. They might just put a slightly larger fraction of their resources into making copies of themselves, or acquiring more resources. Over a long enough period, those differences can dominate. And the things we actually care about—having interesting experiences, maintaining relationships, doing science for its own sake—aren’t necessarily the things that help you win that competition.

The obvious way out is coordination: some arrangement that prevents that dynamic from taking over. But then the question is whether you can enforce it at the largest scale. If different parts of civilisation are very far apart and communication is slow, that seems difficult. So my worry is less that everyone will choose competition, and more that competition could determine what survives even when almost nobody particularly wants it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordination and limits but says nothing about historical attempts to lock in values or their failure.

r002.rationale: The response describes competition between independent groups, but does not propose that adding levels of civilisation scaffolding adds levels of competition.
